 Montgomery County election officials are continuing work to tally and certify ballots for the Nov. 3 general election. Bryant Billing / Staff
 Bryant Billing / Staff 
 The Montgomery County Board of Elections will begin its official canvass of ballots from the Nov. 3 general election this week — and election officials are tasked with sorting through and counting more than 4,000 provisional and other ballots during that process.
 Montgomery County Board of Elections Director Jeff Rezabek during a Friday, Nov. 6 press conference said that the official canvass is slated to begin on Monday.
 More than 204,000 Montgomery County ballots were cast during the Nov. 3 general election. Another 4,418 ballots were cast provisionally — provisional ballots aren’t reflected in an election night unofficial count because they require another layer of security.
 These ballots will help determine the fate of a few close races locally.
 Montgomery County election officials will begin the official canvass of election results starting Monday, Nov. 9. SYDNEY DAWES/STAFF
 SYDNEY DAWES/STAFF 
 State Rep. Tom Young, R-Washington Twp., appears to have lost reelection to Democrat Tom Herner, according to final, unofficial election results. But the margin makes the race too close to call. Young trails Herner by only 134 votes. His seat represents much of southern Montgomery County.
 If Montgomery County’s final margin after all ballots are counted is less than one-half of a percent, an automatic recount will be triggered.
 The Montgomery County Board of Elections shared at least 612 ballots in the 37th House District remain uncounted. This figure does not include provisional ballots, but does include Election Day curbside voting, outstanding military and overseas ballots and other ballots.
 “If there are very close races, we will do our utmost to make sure it’s transparent with each step of the process,” Rezabek said.
 Another issue that could come down to provisional ballots is the levy for Dayton Public Schools, which appears to be failing by 593 votes.
 This issue would generate $14.7 million for Montgomery County’s largest school district if passed.
 Provisional, other ballots
 Montgomery County election officials estimated that roughly 75% of provisional ballots are deemed valid and are thus counted each election. For this election, the board will review 4,418 provisional ballots.
 “Don’t be discouraged if we tell you to vote provisionally. It’s probably going to count,” Rezabek said.
 The “cure” period for provisional ballots ended Saturday, Nov. 7. This is the period where people who voted on a provisional ballot can take additional steps to prove their identity. In many cases, this is simply showing an unexpired, government-issued photo ID card.
 But provisional ballots aren’t the only outstanding ballots awaiting to join the final, official count. Nearly 190 military and overseas ballots are outstanding, with another 117 ballots falling in the 11-S category — this means absentee ballots that are missing a signature or other identifying information that prevents an election board from processing it.
 These voters are contacted by their local election board and have the same deadline as provisional voters to cure their ballots.
 According to the Ohio Secretary of State, election boards across the state may begin their official canvass of Nov. 3 election results on Sunday, Nov. 8. Election boards must complete that official canvass no later than Tuesday, Nov. 24.
